doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Parents: father's finance business and mother the pianist
summary: Igoe describes his Irish-descended father's finance company, his mother's concert piano and practice habits, and his own drums-only focus.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: What did your parents do for a living? Your father?

My father was in a business he hated. He was the manager of a finance company in Jersey City. It was a family business. His father and I think his mother too, well my grandmother, I don’t know if she was born in Jersey City. But he came over from Ireland

as a young man, his father, my grandfather, came over from Ireland. And he started this business. He was a smart guy I guess. He started this business, he had license number three in New Jersey for all the finance companies in New Jersey. He had number three. So my father, when he died my father had to run the business. And he hated that. He didn’t like it. And so anyway that’s what he did. My mother, like all mothers back then, she was home all the time. But she was a very fine classical pianist. We had a full-sized concert grand in our living room. And boy, she used to have concerts there and they’d bring people out from New York who were supposed to be good and all that kind of stuff. They had like a music club. And they’d bring people out from New York. And I would be above the piano in my bedroom, and I could hear some of these people and think boy, it sounds like he’s clubbing it. And then my mother would play and her touch was so much better than a lot of them. Here she was a housewife, but she was a practicing fool. I tell people this story because talk about practice — she had small hands, she couldn’t reach that far. So she was constantly doing these kind of exercises to get loose. And she had this system. She’d put a hundred matches here. Okay? On this side of the piano. And she’s trying a certain thing from a certain concerto. Down and up. Okay put one match over there. [scats] Another match over there. A hundred on this side, then a hundred from that side up on another portion the way she — that may be where I got my practice ethic. Because in high school I used to practice four to six hours a day myself all the time. I wasn’t scholastically great. Because I had blinders on. Everything was drums and everybody knew it was going to be drums.
So there wasn’t much doubt what you were going to be doing for a living.
Oh absolutely, absolutely. My father — as long as Gene Krupa was in charge so to speak, of sending me to a teacher and saying that he thought I had the stuff that I could make a go of it, you know.
